basic_information.name: EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)
basic_information.effective_date: Entered into force 1 August 2024; phased application: prohibited practices from 2 February 2025, GPAI obligations from 2 August 2025, most remaining rules from 2 August 2026, high-risk AI in regulated products from 2 August 2027

scope_and_content.summary: The world's first comprehensive legal framework regulating artificial intelligence, adopting a risk-based approach that classifies AI systems into four tiers (unacceptable, high, limited, minimal risk) with proportionate obligations. It covers AI providers, deployers, importers, and distributors, with special rules for General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models including foundation models. The Act aims to ensure AI systems in the EU are safe, transparent, traceable, non-discriminatory, and environmentally friendly while fostering innovation.
key_provisions: Risk-based classification system with four tiers: unacceptable (banned), high-risk (strict obligations), limited risk (transparency), and minimal risk (no restrictions)

Eight prohibited AI practices including social scoring, subliminal manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces (with limited law enforcement exceptions), emotion recognition in workplaces/schools, untargeted scraping for facial recognition databases, and biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes
High-risk AI systems must comply with risk management, data governance, technical documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity requirements
Conformity assessment required for high-risk systems before market placement, with CE marking
Transparency obligations for AI systems interacting with persons (chatbots must disclose AI nature), and for deepfakes/synthetic content (must be labelled)
GPAI model obligations: technical documentation, copyright compliance policy, publicly available training data summary
GPAI models with systemic risk (>10^25 FLOPs threshold): additional obligations including model evaluation, adversarial testing, incident reporting, cybersecurity protections
Code of Practice for GPAI providers (final version published July 2025) as voluntary compliance mechanism
AI literacy obligation: providers and deployers must ensure staff have sufficient AI competence (applicable since February 2025)
Mandatory AI regulatory sandboxes: each Member State must establish at least one by August 2026
Serious incident reporting to national authorities and AI Office without undue delay
EU database registration for high-risk AI systems
scope_and_content.risk_classification: Four-tier risk framework: (1) Unacceptable risk - 8 banned practices violating fundamental rights; (2) High risk - safety components of regulated products (Annex I, e.g. medical devices, machinery) and stand-alone systems in 8 sensitive domains (Annex III: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration/border, justice/democracy); (3) Limited risk - transparency obligations for AI interacting with persons, deepfakes, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation; (4) Minimal risk - no mandatory obligations (e.g. spam filters, AI in video games). Separate regime for GPAI models with systemic risk threshold at 10^25 FLOPs of training compute.
scope_and_content.covered_entities: Providers (developers) of AI systems and GPAI models regardless of location if placed on EU market; deployers (users) established or located in the EU; importers and distributors; product manufacturers integrating AI; authorised representatives of non-EU providers. Excludes: AI for purely military/defence purposes, AI used exclusively for scientific R&D, free and open-source AI below systemic risk threshold (partial exemption), and AI systems released under free licenses before being put on the market.
scope_and_content.sector_scope: Horizontal regulation applying across all sectors, with specific high-risk designations for: biometrics, critical infrastructure (transport, energy, water, digital), education, employment and worker management, essential public/private services (social benefits, credit scoring, insurance, emergency services), law enforcement, migration/asylum/border control, and administration of justice/democratic processes. Exemptions: military/defence, scientific R&D (pre-market), personal non-professional use.
scope_and_content.open_source_treatment: Partial exemption for GPAI models released under qualifying free and open-source licenses (must allow access, use, modification, redistribution; weights, architecture, and usage info must be publicly available). Exempt from: technical documentation requirements (Art. 53(1a)-(1b)) and information provision to downstream providers. NOT exempt from: copyright compliance policy and training data summary publication. Critical limitation: open-source GPAI models classified as having systemic risk (>10^25 FLOPs) receive NO exemptions and must comply with all obligations. The July 2025 GPAI Guidelines clarified that monetisation of the model itself (not downstream services) may void the open-source exemption.
scope_and_content.extraterritorial_reach: Applies to entities outside the EU under three conditions (Article 2(1)): (a) providers placing AI systems or GPAI models on the EU market, regardless of establishment location; (b) deployers located in a third country where the AI system's output is used in the EU; (c) importers and distributors. Similar to GDPR's extraterritorial scope. Non-EU providers must appoint an authorised representative in the EU. The 'output-based' jurisdiction in Art. 2(1)(c) is particularly broad — if an AI system's output is used within the EU, even if both provider and deployer are outside the EU, the Act may apply.

compliance_and_enforcement.penalties: Three-tier fine structure: (1) Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover (whichever is higher) for violations of prohibited AI practices; (2) Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover for non-compliance with other obligations (high-risk requirements, GPAI rules, etc.); (3) Up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% of worldwide annual turnover for supplying incorrect/misleading information to authorities. For SMEs and startups, the lower of the two amounts (fixed or percentage) applies as a cap. For EU institutions/bodies: EUR 1.5 million for prohibited practices, EUR 750,000 for other violations. GPAI-specific fines under Art. 101: up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover.
compliance_and_enforcement.enforcement_body: Dual-level enforcement: (1) National market surveillance authorities in each Member State handle AI system compliance; (2) European AI Office (within DG Connect, European Commission) has exclusive jurisdiction over GPAI model obligations. AI Office headed by Director Lucilla Sioli, with 140+ staff across 5 units. Additional governance: European AI Board (Member State representatives), Advisory Forum (stakeholders), Scientific Panel of independent experts.
compliance_and_enforcement.compliance_timeline: Phased over 3 years: 2 Feb 2025 - prohibited practices ban and AI literacy obligations apply; 2 Aug 2025 - GPAI model obligations, governance rules, and Code of Practice apply; 2 Aug 2026 - most remaining rules apply including high-risk AI systems under Annex III, transparency obligations, penalties regime (except GPAI penalties which started Aug 2025); 2 Aug 2027 - high-risk AI systems embedded in regulated products under Annex I (medical devices, machinery, etc.) and legacy GPAI models (placed on market before Aug 2025) must comply. NOTE: Digital Omnibus proposal (Nov 2025) may extend high-risk deadlines by up to 16 months pending adoption.
compliance_and_enforcement.reporting_requirements: High-risk AI systems: (1) Technical documentation demonstrating compliance before market placement; (2) EU declaration of conformity; (3) Registration in EU database; (4) Serious incident reporting to national authorities without undue delay; (5) Post-market monitoring system; (6) Quality management system documentation; (7) Logging and traceability capabilities. GPAI models: (1) Technical documentation including training/testing process info and evaluation results; (2) Sufficiently detailed training data summary (template published Aug 2025); (3) Copyright policy documentation; (4) Systemic risk models: adversarial testing results, incident reporting to AI Office. Deployers of high-risk AI: (1) Fundamental rights impact assessment for public bodies; (2) Monitoring obligations; (3) Data input record-keeping.
compliance_and_enforcement.sme_provisions: Dedicated provisions under Articles 57-62: (1) Priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes for SMEs and startups, provided free of charge with simplified procedures; (2) Proportionate conformity assessment fees based on size and development stage; (3) Commission commitment to regularly review and reduce compliance costs; (4) Member States must provide tailored guidance, training, and awareness activities; (5) Dedicated communication channels for SME questions; (6) Support for participation in standardisation processes; (7) Real-world testing within sandboxes with safe harbour from fines if following guidance in good faith; (8) Digital Omnibus proposal (Nov 2025) adds: simplified technical documentation for SMEs/SMCs, proportionate quality management obligations, and penalty mitigation for smaller entities.
compliance_and_enforcement.liability_model: product_liability (primary), with fault-based elements. The AI Act itself is primarily a product safety regulation (not a liability law), but non-compliance creates strong liability exposure through: (1) New Product Liability Directive (in force Dec 2024) — non-compliance with mandatory safety requirements creates a rebuttable presumption of defect, triggering strict liability; (2) The proposed AI Liability Directive (which would have introduced reversed burden of proof for fault-based claims) was WITHDRAWN by the Commission in February 2025 due to lack of consensus, leaving a regulatory gap in fault-based AI liability; (3) Existing national tort law regimes remain applicable. Net result: strict product liability via PLD for AI-as-product, but no harmonised fault-based liability framework for AI-as-service.

impact_and_analysis.business_impact: Differential impact by company size: LARGE ENTERPRISES face significant but manageable compliance costs, most already have legal/compliance teams and can absorb the estimated EUR 52,000/year per high-risk AI system; many large US tech companies will comply voluntarily to maintain EU market access (de facto Brussels effect). STARTUPS AND SMEs face disproportionate burden — compliance costs estimated at $160,000-$330,000 per high-risk system, potentially consuming a significant share of early-stage funding; 18-50% of AI systems may qualify as high-risk (far exceeding the Commission's original 5-15% estimate). The compliance market itself is projected to reach EUR 17 billion by 2030, creating new business opportunities. Key concerns: (1) Classification uncertainty — unclear risk categorisation causes businesses to hesitate in AI adoption; (2) First-mover disadvantage — EU companies face compliance costs that non-EU competitors avoid; (3) Talent flight risk — founders warn of driving talent abroad; (4) Positive effects — compliance-as-a-service market, trust premium for EU AI companies, regulatory clarity enabling investment. The Digital Omnibus proposal (Nov 2025) attempts to address these concerns through extended timelines and simplified requirements for smaller entities.
impact_and_analysis.innovation_effect: Mixed evidence. CONSTRAINING factors: (1) 56 EU AI companies including Mistral AI and Aleph Alpha signed a July 2025 letter urging the Commission to 'pause and simplify' parts of the Act; (2) Compliance costs divert R&D spending; (3) Open letter from European CEOs requested a two-year 'clock-stop' citing negative impact on competitiveness; (4) Classification uncertainty creates regulatory chill — businesses hesitate to deploy AI. PROMOTING factors: (1) Regulatory sandboxes (mandatory in each Member State by Aug 2026) enable controlled experimentation; (2) Regulatory clarity may attract investment from risk-averse sectors; (3) EU AI companies may gain a trust and safety premium in global markets; (4) Apply AI Strategy (Oct 2025) and AI Continent Action Plan invest in European AI capabilities; (5) EUR 17B compliance market creates new innovation opportunities. Net assessment: short-term innovation drag likely, long-term effects depend on implementation quality and whether sandboxes/simplification measures prove effective.
impact_and_analysis.global_influence: The 'Brussels effect' for the AI Act is more limited than for GDPR. EVIDENCE OF INFLUENCE: (1) Brazil and Canada are drafting similar risk-based AI frameworks; (2) Large US tech companies will likely comply voluntarily for EU market access (de facto Brussels effect); (3) The GPAI Code of Practice may influence global AI safety norms; (4) Some scholars see it as a template for future international standards. LIMITATIONS: (1) Unlike GDPR, the AI Act faces competition from alternative regulatory models — UK, Japan, Singapore, Australia pursuing pro-innovation, less prescriptive approaches; (2) US under current administration is pursuing deregulation; (3) China has its own AI regulation model (state-control oriented); (4) Only 2 countries (Canada, Brazil) actively emulating the EU approach; (5) Brookings analysis: 'Europe alone will not be setting a comprehensive new international standard for AI'; (6) The EU itself is already walking back provisions via the Digital Omnibus, potentially undermining its regulatory authority.
impact_and_analysis.stakeholder_positions: INDUSTRY: Generally critical of complexity and costs. 56 EU AI companies (including Mistral AI, Aleph Alpha) signed July 2025 open letter urging pause/simplification. European CEO coalition requested two-year 'clock-stop'. Startup community warns of competitiveness loss and talent flight. France's position was heavily influenced by Mistral AI's lobbyist Cedric O (former Secretary of State for Digital Transition), who called the Act 'the death sentence of artificial intelligence in Europe'. CIVIL SOCIETY: Concerned that simplification efforts erode protections. CDT's Laura Cabrera: 'Postponing enforcement leaves people unprotected from harms of high-risk AI systems'. Article 19, Access Now, and other rights organisations argue the Code of Practice was watered down by industry lobbying. Corporate Europe Observatory documented Big Tech's outsized influence on negotiations. ACADEMIA: Mixed views — some scholars support the risk-based framework as proportionate, others warn of innovation drag. MEMBER STATES: France favoured lighter touch for GPAI (influenced by Mistral/national champions), Germany pushed for stronger SME protections, smaller states concerned about enforcement capacity.
impact_and_analysis.deregulatory_signals: Yes, significant deregulatory signals emerging since mid-2025. MECHANISMS: (1) Digital Omnibus proposal (Nov 2025) — extends high-risk AI deadlines by up to 16 months, adds SME/SMC simplifications, introduces EU-level regulatory sandbox, extends generative AI compliance deadline to Feb 2027; (2) Industry pressure — CEO letter requesting two-year 'clock-stop', open letters from 56 AI companies; (3) Commission rhetoric shift — emphasis on 'simplification' and 'competitiveness' (aligned with Draghi Report recommendations); (4) AI Liability Directive withdrawal (Feb 2025) — removed planned fault-based liability harmonisation; (5) Apply AI Strategy and AI Continent Action Plan (Oct 2025) signal pivot toward 'AI adoption' narrative. However, the core Act structure (risk tiers, prohibited practices) remains intact — the deregulatory signals primarily target implementation speed and compliance burden rather than fundamental architecture.

related_regulations: GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) — data protection framework, AI systems must comply with GDPR for personal data processing
Product Liability Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/2853) — non-compliance with AI Act safety requirements creates rebuttable presumption of defect
AI Liability Directive — WITHDRAWN by Commission in February 2025, would have harmonised fault-based AI liability with reversed burden of proof
General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988 — complements AI Act for consumer-facing AI products
Cyber Resilience Act — cybersecurity requirements for digital products including AI
Digital Services Act (DSA) — platform regulation, overlaps with AI Act on recommender systems and content moderation
EU Copyright Directive (2019/790) — GPAI providers must comply with text and data mining rules
EU AI Act Digital Omnibus (proposed Nov 2025) — simplification amendments currently in legislative process
OECD AI Principles — international framework referenced in AI Act design
EU AI Pact — voluntary initiative preceding mandatory AI Act obligations
key_actors: European Commission (DG Connect) — proposed the Act (April 2021), oversees implementation
European Parliament — co-legislator, key rapporteurs Brando Benifei (S&D, Italy) and Dragos Tudorache (Renew, Romania)
Council of the EU — co-legislator, Spanish Presidency brokered final political agreement (Dec 2023)
Thierry Breton — former Commissioner for Internal Market, championed the initial AI Act proposal
Lucilla Sioli — Director of the European AI Office (140+ staff), leads GPAI enforcement
Mistral AI — French AI startup, major lobbying force for lighter GPAI obligations through Cedric O
Cedric O — Mistral AI lobbyist, former French Secretary of State for Digital Transition, influenced French negotiating position
Mario Draghi — his competitiveness report reinforced narrative for regulatory simplification
European AI Board — representatives from 27 Member States for cross-border coordination
Advisory Forum — multi-stakeholder body (industry, civil society, academia) advising Commission
Scientific Panel of Independent Experts — advises on GPAI model classification and systemic risk
recent_developments: 2 Feb 2025: Prohibited AI practices ban and AI literacy obligations became applicable — first enforcement milestone
11 Feb 2025: European Commission withdrew the AI Liability Directive proposal, citing lack of consensus
2 Aug 2025: GPAI model obligations became applicable; rules for governance structures took effect; Code of Practice for GPAI published in final form (July 2025)
18 Jul 2025: Commission published draft Guidelines for GPAI model providers, clarifying definitions and scope
Jul 2025: 56 EU AI companies including Mistral AI signed open letter urging Commission to simplify/pause parts of the Act
Oct 2025: Commission launched Apply AI Strategy complementing AI Continent Action Plan, targeting AI adoption by SMEs
19 Nov 2025: European Commission published Digital Omnibus on AI proposal — proposes extending high-risk deadlines by up to 16 months, adding EU-level regulatory sandbox, simplifying SME obligations
Jan 2026: Multiple Member States working on national AI sandbox frameworks ahead of Aug 2026 deadline
Feedback period on Digital Omnibus open until 9 March 2026; legislative process in Council and Parliament ongoing
As of Feb 2026: High-risk AI system rules (Annex III) scheduled for 2 Aug 2026 but may be delayed by Digital Omnibus adoption

teaching_relevance.entrepreneurial_implications: Critical for any AI startup targeting European markets. KEY IMPLICATIONS: (1) COMPLIANCE COSTS — estimated EUR 52,000/year per high-risk AI system for conformity assessment, documentation, and monitoring; startups face $160,000-$330,000 total compliance costs, potentially requiring dedicated compliance hires or external consultants; (2) MARKET ACCESS — the Act's extraterritorial reach means even non-EU startups must comply if their AI outputs are used in the EU, creating a compliance barrier to entry but also a level playing field; (3) COMPETITIVE MOATS — compliance creates a trust premium and barrier to entry that benefits first-movers who invest in safety/transparency; EU-compliant AI products may command premium pricing in regulated sectors (healthcare, finance, HR); (4) BUSINESS MODEL IMPACT — some AI use cases are outright banned (social scoring, manipulative AI), others require heavy investment in human oversight and documentation; B2B AI companies must provide downstream deployers with sufficient information; (5) SANDBOX OPPORTUNITY — regulatory sandboxes offer startups a way to test innovative AI under regulatory guidance with safe harbour from fines; SMEs get priority access and fee waivers; (6) TIMING STRATEGY — the phased rollout and Digital Omnibus delays create a window for startups to prepare; understanding the timeline is a genuine competitive advantage; (7) OPEN SOURCE STRATEGY — releasing models under open licenses reduces some obligations but not all (copyright compliance still required), and systemic risk models get no exemptions regardless; (8) COMPLIANCE-AS-A-SERVICE — the EUR 17B compliance market creates startup opportunities in AI governance tools, auditing, documentation automation, and risk classification services.
teaching_relevance.session_mapping: Session 5 (Ethics, governance & final presentations) — primary session for EU AI Act coverage. Also relevant to Session 3 (Framing & managing AI projects) for risk classification and compliance planning, and Session 4 (AI business models & strategy) for understanding regulatory impact on business model viability and market access.

confidence.data_quality: High — based on official EU legal texts (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), European Commission publications, European Parliament briefings, and analysis from major law firms (Orrick, DLA Piper, WilmerHale, Cooley). Timeline and penalty figures drawn directly from the Act's articles.
confidence.cross_reference: European Commission official pages (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu), artificialintelligenceact.eu (independent reference), EU AI Act Service Desk (ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu), European Parliament research service, Brookings Institution, CSIS, Carnegie Endowment, Corporate Europe Observatory, IAPP, Chatham House. Compliance cost estimates cross-referenced between CEPS, EU impact assessment, and industry surveys.
confidence.caveats: The regulatory landscape is actively evolving: (1) The Digital Omnibus on AI (proposed Nov 2025) is in legislative process and could significantly alter implementation timelines and requirements — feedback period open until March 2026; (2) The AI Liability Directive withdrawal (Feb 2025) leaves a gap in fault-based liability that may be revisited; (3) GPAI systemic risk threshold (10^25 FLOPs) may be revised as compute capabilities evolve; (4) National implementation varies — Member States have discretion in penalty structures and sandbox design; (5) The Commission's GPAI Guidelines (July 2025) are non-binding and may be challenged; (6) Compliance cost estimates vary widely (5-50% of AI systems as high-risk depending on methodology); (7) Standardisation work by CEN/CENELEC for harmonised standards is ongoing and will materially affect compliance requirements.
